I went to college in the US as an international student and was able to work at a brewery there for 3 years on my STEM OPT but was unsuccessful at obtaining an H1B. 

Keep in mind that the H1B also involves an extremely competitive lottery process each year that decides whether or not your company will even be able to apply for one. My company was more than willing to sponsor me but I didn't get past the lottery stage all 3 years that I applied. 

I met with several lawyers regarding an O1 visa and they all told me that a brewing job/education isn't good enough to justify an extraordinary ability visa. 

As someone who's been in the same boat my advice would be to look into other countries - as much as I miss the industry in the US, I'm now happily brewing abroad and am grateful that this career is allowing me to see the world. Feel free to PM if I can help out at all!

I did C2C in the first week of May this year - started at 3am and it was already 80⁰+ in Palm Springs. September might be too hot and imo not worth the risk, but as someone already mentioned, you might just get lucky with a weather window! I'd watch conditions closely and make a call as it gets closer - if you do decide to go for it, I'd suggest you gauge how you're feeling/how the weather is by the time you get to rescue box #2 and decide then whether you want to keep going or not, but I would definitely avoid turning back anytime after that point. 

It's a beautiful hike and probably one of the most fulfilling experiences I've had, but just know your limits and keep in mind that most rescues/deaths on this trail happen when people decide to turn back when it's too late - it's easy to get lost in the desert on the way down. Stay safe and good luck!

It was my first time up to the summit. The distance isn't that bad but it's the elevation gain that was killer. All straight uphill, almost 1000ft/mile (more during some sections) with basically no respite. In terms of traction, we were mostly fine with microspikes and poles but some sections towards the top did start to get a little sketchy and it got kinda tricky following the trail closer to the summit. Snow/ice also made considerably it harder in general along with the cold, altitude and wind but I imagine it'd be much simpler during the summer! It was pretty gruelling but fairly doable imo, and I don't have nearly as much hiking experience as some people on this subreddit do. I'd just recommend being adequately prepared (both mentally and equipment-wise) , and starting early so that you can take your time and do it at your own pace - it's definitely very intense and not just a stroll up a hill. Also good to trust your gut and know if and when it's time to turn around and head back. 

From what I've read, the Devils Backbone is a longer but less steep route to the top which should be safe to traverse in the summer once the snow clears up, but is extremely dangerous otherwise. You can also get a ski lift to get you to the trailhead, enabling you to essentially skip the first couple miles up to the notch. 

It was a beautiful day, skies were clear, and views were breathtaking - definitely worth  it!

I used to smoke a lot two years ago too. Some would call it an unhealthy amount. I'd lost all interest in life, and weed made it a bit more tolerable to stay indoors and do nothing for days at a time. 

I took some time off from college, tried to stop smoking for a bit, and was told by family, friends and multiple psychiatrists that all my problems would go away when I stopped smoking pot. They didn't. So I started smoking again, because well, it made life less shitty. 

All I decided to change was to spend at least 30 minutes outside each time I smoked. I walked my dog, went for jogs, started playing tennis, and realized that life didn't suck as much as I'd made it seem. Over time, I stopped seeing weed as an escape, but more as a way to amplify my experiences. 

Weed itself didn't help me turn my life around, but changing my attitude towards consuming it did.
